question_text: A data engineering team needs to validate documents before ingesting them into a Bedrock Knowledge Base. They need automated quality scoring and metadata-level issue detection. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Macie
AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Config

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality lets you define DQDL rules for completeness, freshness, uniqueness, and custom logic — directly applicable to pre-ingestion document validation as cited in Skill 1.3.1. Amazon Macie detects PII/sensitive data but does not score general data quality. GuardDuty is a threat-detection service. AWS Config monitors resource configuration compliance, not dataset quality.
source_topic: AWS Glue Data Quality, FM data pipeline

question_text: A company is building a knowledge base from audio call recordings, scanned PDFs, and structured spreadsheets. Which pipeline correctly processes all three data types before FM ingestion?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe for audio → Textract or Glue for PDFs → Bedrock multimodal models for spreadsheet understanding
Amazon Rekognition for audio → Amazon QuickSight for PDFs → Amazon Polly for spreadsheets
Amazon Polly for audio → S3 static hosting for PDFs → Athena for spreadsheets
SageMaker Processing for audio → DynamoDB for PDFs → Lambda for spreadsheets

explanation: Skill 1.3.2 cites Amazon Transcribe for audio and Bedrock multimodal models for complex multimodal pipelines. Transcribe converts speech to text; Textract/Glue extracts text from scanned PDFs; Bedrock multimodal models can interpret tabular/spreadsheet content. Rekognition is for image/video (not audio). Polly converts text to speech — the wrong direction. SageMaker Processing can do audio work but Transcribe is the managed, purpose-built service.
source_topic: Amazon Transcribe, Bedrock multimodal, data processing

question_text: What format must the request body use when calling the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API?

options.text: XML with a model-specific root element
Protocol Buffers (protobuf)
JSON following the model-specific request schema
YAML front matter with a markdown body

explanation: Skill 1.3.3 states: 'Format input data for FM inference using JSON formatting for Amazon Bedrock API requests.' Each Bedrock model has its own JSON schema (e.g., Claude's messages array, Titan's inputText), but the serialisation format is always JSON. XML, protobuf, and YAML are not supported by the Bedrock API.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API, JSON

question_text: A developer is building a multi-turn chatbot using the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. How should prior conversation turns be included in each request?

options.text: Concatenate all prior messages into one plain-text string in the user field
Pass a messages array with alternating user and assistant role entries; add a system field for persistent instructions
Rely on Bedrock's built-in session memory — the API automatically recalls past turns
Use session cookies to transmit conversation state

explanation: Skill 1.3.3 cites 'conversation formatting for dialog-based applications.' The Bedrock Converse API accepts a messages array with alternating user/assistant role turns and an optional top-level system field. The API is stateless — each request must carry the full conversation history. Concatenating into a single string loses role structure. Session cookies are a browser mechanism, not an FM API construct.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock Converse API, conversation formatting

question_text: A chatbot produces inconsistent answers because user inputs contain informal abbreviations, inconsistent casing, and mixed-language tokens. Which preprocessing steps improve response quality? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to extract named entities and standardise terminology
Use Lambda functions to normalise and clean text before FM invocation
Use Amazon Rekognition to detect inappropriate content in text
Use Amazon Polly to re-read text aloud and re-transcribe for better quality
Use Amazon Translate to force all input to English before FM invocation

explanation: Skill 1.3.4 lists Amazon Comprehend (entity extraction and text standardisation) and Lambda (normalisation functions) for enhancing input quality. Rekognition is for images/video — not text content. Polly→re-transcription adds latency with no quality benefit for already-text input. Force-translating to English would lose meaning for multilingual use cases and is not listed as a recommended approach.
source_topic: Amazon Comprehend, Lambda, input preprocessing

topic: SageMaker Data Wrangler for FM prep
question_text: A data scientist needs to profile, transform, and visually explore a dataset before fine-tuning an FM, without writing custom ETL code. Which service provides a GUI for this task?

options.text: Amazon Athena
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
AWS Glue Studio
Amazon QuickSight

explanation: Skill 1.3.1 cites SageMaker Data Wrangler as a tool for data validation workflows. Data Wrangler provides a visual interface for profiling, transforming, and quality-checking datasets — purpose-built for ML/FM preparation. Athena is a SQL engine with no visual prep UI. Glue Studio is a visual ETL builder for data engineering pipelines. QuickSight is a BI tool for dashboards and analytics, not data preparation.
source_topic: SageMaker Data Wrangler, FM fine-tuning data prep

question_text: A developer wants the FM to always return a JSON object with specific fields (customer_name, order_id, sentiment) for CRM integration. How should the prompt be structured?

options.text: Ask the FM in natural language to 'return something structured'
Provide a JSON Schema definition and few-shot examples in the prompt; instruct the FM to strictly follow the schema
Post-process the FM's free-form output with regex to extract values
Use Amazon Textract to parse the FM's output as if it were a form document

explanation: Skill 1.3.3 cites 'structured data preparation' and 1.3.1 mentions 'JSON Schema to enforce structured outputs'. Providing a JSON Schema and few-shot examples is the most reliable technique for constrained output formatting — the FM learns the exact schema from examples and the schema constrains its output. Vague natural-language instructions produce inconsistent formats. Regex post-processing is brittle for varied FM outputs. Textract is for extracting data from PDFs/images, not parsing FM text.
source_topic: JSON Schema, structured FM output, few-shot prompting

question_text: A team wants to monitor the health of their FM data ingestion pipeline — specifically detecting when documents fail validation checks. Which AWS service should they use to set up automated alerts?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie

explanation: Skill 1.3.1 lists Amazon CloudWatch metrics as part of data validation workflows. Publishing custom metrics (e.g., failed_validation_count) to CloudWatch and creating alarms with SNS notifications is the standard operational monitoring pattern on AWS. Trusted Advisor is for best-practice recommendations. Inspector scans for vulnerabilities. Macie detects sensitive data — not pipeline health.
source_topic: Amazon CloudWatch, data pipeline monitoring

question_text: A company receives invoices from 400 different vendors, each with a different layout and different column names for totals. They need normalised JSON output from every invoice with minimal custom code. Which service is most appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Textract key-value extraction
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation — uses GenAI to understand context across irregular multi-format documents
AWS Glue DataBrew profiling job
Amazon Comprehend entity recognition

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation uses GenAI to understand semantic context across documents with highly variable layouts ('Amount Due' = 'Total' = 'Balance Due'), outputting normalised JSON — directly cited in Skill 1.3.2 for automated data processing workflows. Textract is fast and accurate for fixed-template or well-structured forms but cannot handle extreme layout variability. Glue DataBrew processes structured datasets. Comprehend extracts named entities but does not normalise them into a domain-specific schema.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation, Amazon Textract

topic: Kinesis Firehose for streaming data ingestion
question_text: A company streams millions of IoT sensor events per second to S3 for later RAG ingestion. They need auto-compression, date-based partitioning, and zero custom processing code. Which service delivers this?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a custom Lambda consumer
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose — auto-buffers, compresses, date-partitions, and delivers to S3 without code
Amazon MSK with a self-managed Kafka consumer
AWS Glue streaming ETL with a PySpark script

explanation: Kinesis Data Firehose is the no-code streaming-to-S3 funnel: it automatically buffers, compresses (GZIP/Snappy), partitions by date, and delivers to S3 (Skill 1.3.2 — data processing workflows for FM consumption). Data Streams requires writing and maintaining a consumer (Lambda). MSK requires managing Kafka brokers and writing consumer code. A Glue streaming job requires PySpark/Scala code — higher operational effort.
source_topic: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, FM data pipeline

question_text: A company stores internal documentation in Atlassian Confluence and public product pages on a company website. A developer is building a Bedrock Knowledge Base and needs to ingest both sources. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Configure separate Bedrock Knowledge Base data source connectors — one for Confluence and one using the web crawler — to ingest both sources
Manually download all Confluence pages as PDFs weekly and upload them to S3
Embed the website content directly into the system prompt on every invocation
Store all content in DynamoDB and write a custom Lambda to forward it to the model

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides managed data source connectors for Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, and a web crawler. Using the dedicated connectors automates ingestion and keeps the index up to date. Manual weekly exports, stuffing the system prompt with a full website, and routing DynamoDB records via Lambda are all unscalable workarounds that bypass the purpose-built connectors.
source_topic: Bedrock Knowledge Bases data source connectors

topic: GDPR right to erasure in vector stores
question_text: A European user invokes their GDPR right to erasure. The company's Bedrock Knowledge Base contains chunks from documents that include that user's data. Which sequence of steps FULLY satisfies the erasure requirement?

options.text: Delete the source documents containing the user's data from the S3 data source, then re-sync the knowledge base so the corresponding vectors are purged from the index
Lower the retrieval top-k so the user's chunks are less likely to appear
Add a guardrail word filter blocking the user's name
Rotate the KMS key used to encrypt the vector store

explanation: The only way to fully erase data from a RAG pipeline is to delete the source records and re-sync (re-index) the knowledge base so the derived vectors are also removed. Reducing top-k merely reduces the probability the data appears — it is still present and retrievable. A word filter blocks the name string but not other personal data in the chunks. Rotating the KMS key re-encrypts existing data but does not delete it.
source_topic: GDPR erasure, data deletion in knowledge bases

question_text: A legal team's archive consists entirely of scanned paper documents saved as image-only PDFs. When the team tries to ingest them into a Bedrock Knowledge Base, no text content is returned in retrieval results. What is the root cause and the correct remediation?

options.text: The PDFs have no extractable text layer; an OCR step must be added in the ingestion pipeline (e.g., via Amazon Textract) to extract text before embedding
The embedding model dimension is too small; increase it
The chunks are too large; reduce chunk size to one word
The knowledge base needs a higher temperature setting

explanation: Image-only PDFs contain no machine-readable text, so a standard text extractor produces nothing. Adding OCR — for example using Amazon Textract during pre-processing — converts the scanned images to text, which can then be chunked and embedded. Embedding dimension, chunk size, and temperature are unrelated to the absence of a text layer.
source_topic: Amazon Textract, OCR pipeline for knowledge base ingestion

question_text: A machine learning team wants to fine-tune a large foundation model on domain-specific data without updating all model weights, to minimize storage and compute cost. Which technique achieves this?

options.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) — trains small low-rank matrices added to frozen base model weights
Full fine-tuning — retrains all layers of the base model
Prompt engineering — modifies only the input text with no weight updates
Model distillation — trains a smaller student model from scratch using teacher model outputs

explanation: LoRA freezes the base model weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices (typically added to attention layers). At inference these are merged with the base weights, producing an adapted model at a fraction of the compute and storage cost of full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning updates all weights. Prompt engineering changes only the input with no training. Distillation creates a new smaller model — it does not adapt an existing one efficiently.
source_topic: LoRA, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Bedrock customization

topic: Amazon MSK for real-time GenAI data ingestion
question_text: A company produces millions of customer events per second (clicks, transactions, sensor readings) and wants to feed this real-time stream into a GenAI pipeline for contextual recommendations. Which AWS service provides a fully managed Apache Kafka cluster for high-throughput event streaming?

options.text: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) — fully managed Kafka for high-throughput, low-latency event streaming
Amazon SQS — a simple message queue not designed for high-throughput streaming
AWS Glue — an ETL service, not a real-time streaming platform
Amazon S3 — object storage without native streaming semantics

explanation: Amazon MSK is a fully managed Apache Kafka service purpose-built for high-throughput, low-latency event streaming at scale. Consumers (including GenAI pipelines) can subscribe to topics and process events in real time. SQS is a simpler queue with lower throughput ceilings and no Kafka semantics. Glue is batch/micro-batch ETL. S3 is object storage with no push-based streaming.
source_topic: Amazon MSK, Kafka, real-time data ingestion for GenAI

topic: Amazon EMR — Spark for large-scale GenAI data prep
question_text: A data engineering team needs to preprocess a 50 TB corpus of text documents — deduplication, tokenisation counting, quality filtering — before fine-tuning an FM. The job should run on a temporary distributed cluster that scales down after completion. Which AWS service is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon EMR with Apache Spark — provides a managed, auto-scaling distributed compute cluster for large-scale data processing jobs
AWS Lambda — serverless functions limited to 15 minutes and 10 GB memory, unsuitable for 50 TB jobs
Amazon RDS — a relational database not designed for distributed data processing
Amazon Comprehend — an NLP service for entity extraction, not distributed ETL

explanation: Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce) provides managed Apache Spark (and Hadoop) clusters that scale to hundreds of nodes for large-scale distributed data processing. It auto-terminates after the job, making it cost-efficient for one-time large corpus preparation. Lambda's 15-minute timeout and 10 GB memory limit make it unsuitable for 50 TB. RDS is a transactional database. Comprehend is an NLP inference service.
source_topic: Amazon EMR, Apache Spark, large-scale GenAI data preparation

question_text: A company needs to extract structured data from thousands of scanned invoices stored in S3 before ingesting them into a Bedrock Knowledge Base. They want to avoid building and maintaining a custom OCR pipeline. Which AWS service is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Textract with custom Lambda post-processing
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) with blueprints
Amazon Rekognition document analysis
AWS Glue ETL with a custom Python script

explanation: Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) with blueprints is specifically designed to extract structured data from unstructured sources (scanned documents, images) without custom OCR code. It integrates natively with Bedrock Knowledge Bases for downstream RAG ingestion. Textract can do OCR but requires custom Lambda post-processing to structure the output. Rekognition is for image/video analysis, not document data extraction. Glue ETL requires building custom parsing logic.
source_topic: Bedrock Data Automation for document ingestion

question_text: A team is designing a pipeline to ingest multimodal content (PDFs with embedded images and text) into a Bedrock Knowledge Base. What is the recommended AWS-native sequence?

options.text: Amazon Textract → Lambda (format) → Bedrock Knowledge Base
Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) → Bedrock Knowledge Base
Amazon Rekognition → Amazon Comprehend → Bedrock Knowledge Base
AWS Glue → Amazon OpenSearch → Bedrock Knowledge Base

explanation: BDA is the recommended AWS-native approach for multimodal ingestion before RAG. It handles both text and image extraction, produces structured output, and integrates directly with Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The Textract → Lambda path works but adds operational overhead. Rekognition + Comprehend is not designed for document-to-KB ingestion. Glue + OpenSearch bypasses the managed KB entirely.
source_topic: Multimodal ingestion: BDA → Knowledge Base

topic: Glue Data Quality for FM pipelines
question_text: Before generating embeddings for a RAG system, a data engineer wants to automatically validate that all document chunks meet quality rules: minimum 50 characters, no null text, correct encoding. Which AWS service BEST provides rule-based data quality validation at scale?

options.text: AWS Lambda with custom validation code
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Macie

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality provides a managed, declarative rule engine for defining and enforcing data quality rules (completeness, format, nulls, schema compliance) across large datasets in S3 or other sources. It produces quality scores and integrates with Glue ETL pipelines. Lambda requires writing all logic manually. SageMaker Data Wrangler is for visual, exploratory data preparation. Macie discovers sensitive data but does not perform structural quality checks.
source_topic: AWS Glue Data Quality for FM data validation

question_text: A company wants to ingest customer data from Salesforce into Amazon S3 for use in a RAG knowledge base, without writing custom integration code. Which AWS service provides managed, no-code data transfer from SaaS applications?

options.text: AWS DataSync
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon AppFlow
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)

explanation: Amazon AppFlow is a fully managed integration service for transferring data between SaaS applications (Salesforce, Slack, Google Analytics, etc.) and AWS services like S3, Redshift, or EventBridge — with no custom code required. DataSync is for file system and storage transfers, not SaaS APIs. Kinesis Firehose handles streaming data, not SaaS connector integration. DMS is for database-to-database migrations.
source_topic: AppFlow for SaaS-to-AWS data ingestion

question_text: A developer notices that a Bedrock Knowledge Base is returning poorly grounded responses. Investigation reveals that some document chunks contain only whitespace or HTML tags. Which pipeline change MOST directly fixes this issue?

options.text: Increase the context window size for the generative model
Switch to a more powerful embedding model
Add data quality rules in AWS Glue to filter out empty or non-textual chunks before embedding
Enable Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks

explanation: The root cause is garbage data (empty/HTML-only chunks) entering the knowledge base. The fix is upstream: add Glue Data Quality rules to filter such chunks before embedding. Larger context windows don't help if the retrieved chunks are meaningless. A better embedding model won't improve vectors of whitespace. Guardrails grounding checks operate at inference time, not at ingestion — they can reduce hallucinations but don't fix corrupt knowledge base data.
source_topic: Upstream data quality for RAG pipelines

question_text: A platform team needs to: (1) catalogue all S3 datasets used in GenAI training and track their lineage, AND (2) restrict which data scientists can query specific columns in those datasets. Which combination of services addresses BOTH requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog (for both cataloguing and access control)
AWS Glue Data Catalog (lineage + metadata) + AWS Lake Formation (column-level access control)
Amazon S3 bucket policies (for access) + AWS Glue Crawlers (for cataloguing)
AWS IAM policies on all S3 objects (for access) + AWS Glue ETL (for lineage)

explanation: Glue Data Catalog handles metadata discovery, table registration, and lineage tracking (what data exists and where it came from). Lake Formation provides fine-grained access control at the column and row level on top of Glue Catalog tables — answering 'who can access what'. S3 bucket policies provide object-level access but not column-level. IAM policies on S3 objects are too coarse for column-level control. Glue ETL is for transformation, not lineage metadata.
source_topic: Glue Data Catalog + Lake Formation combination

question_text: A developer wants to enrich user queries before sending them to a Bedrock model. The enrichment should automatically extract named entities (organizations, dates, locations) from the query to add context to the prompt. Which AWS service provides this capability as a managed API?

options.text: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Textract
Amazon Transcribe

explanation: Amazon Comprehend provides managed NLP APIs for entity extraction, key phrase detection, sentiment analysis, and topic modelling — all without training a custom model. It can extract organizations, dates, locations, and other named entities from text in real time. Rekognition processes images/video, not text NLP. Textract extracts text from documents (OCR), not entities from arbitrary text. Transcribe converts speech to text.
source_topic: Amazon Comprehend entity extraction for prompt enrichment

topic: Kinesis Firehose for streaming data ingestion
question_text: A team needs to continuously ingest real-time product review data from a web application into S3 for periodic Knowledge Base reindexing. The data arrives in a high-volume stream. Which AWS service is MOST appropriate for the ingestion layer?

options.text: Amazon SQS FIFO queue
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
AWS DataSync
Amazon EventBridge Pipes

explanation: Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for near-real-time, high-volume streaming data delivery to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch — with built-in batching, compression, and transformation. It is the standard choice for streaming data ingestion into S3 for downstream processing. SQS is a message queue, not a streaming delivery service to S3. DataSync is for batch file transfers between storage systems. EventBridge Pipes connects event sources to targets but is not optimised for high-volume streaming to S3.
source_topic: Kinesis Firehose for streaming data to S3

question_text: A GenAI application receives raw text from users that often contains typos, inconsistent date formats, and abbreviations. A developer wants to standardize this input before sending it to Bedrock. What is the SIMPLEST approach?

options.text: Use Amazon Kendra to clean and index the text
Use an AWS Lambda function to apply normalization (spell check, date parsing, abbreviation expansion) before invoking Bedrock
Use Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs for each user request
Increase the Bedrock model's temperature to handle noisy inputs

explanation: A Lambda function is the simplest serverless approach for lightweight text normalization (spell-check libraries, date formatting, abbreviation expansion) before passing clean input to Bedrock. It adds minimal latency and no infrastructure overhead. Kendra is a search service, not a text normalizer. SageMaker Processing jobs are batch workloads, not per-request real-time processing. Increasing temperature makes outputs more random, not more robust to noisy inputs.
source_topic: Lambda-based input normalization

question_text: A company wants to build a GenAI pipeline that processes audio recordings of customer calls, summarises each call, and stores summaries in a knowledge base. Which sequence of AWS services is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Polly → Amazon Bedrock → Amazon S3
Amazon Transcribe → AWS Lambda (format) → Amazon Bedrock (summarise) → Amazon S3
Amazon Rekognition → Amazon Comprehend → Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Lex → Amazon Bedrock → Amazon DynamoDB

explanation: Transcribe converts the audio recording to text. Lambda formats and prepares the transcript. Bedrock generates a summary. S3 stores it for later knowledge base ingestion. Polly is text-to-speech (opposite direction). Rekognition processes images/video, not audio. Lex is for building conversational interfaces, not batch audio summarisation pipelines.
source_topic: Audio-to-summary pipeline with Transcribe and Bedrock

question_text: A developer calls the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API but receives a ValidationException. The error states the request body is malformed. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The IAM role does not have bedrock:InvokeModel permission
The request body is not valid JSON or does not match the model's expected schema
The model is not available in the current region
The Lambda function timeout is too short

explanation: A ValidationException on InvokeModel almost always indicates the request body is malformed — either invalid JSON or missing/incorrect required fields for that specific model's schema (e.g., missing 'prompt', wrong field names, incorrect data types). An IAM issue would produce an AccessDeniedException, not a ValidationException. Regional availability produces a ResourceNotFoundException. Lambda timeout produces a TaskTimedOut error, not a ValidationException.
source_topic: Bedrock API request validation

topic: Bedrock Batch Inference for large-scale processing
question_text: A data team needs to generate embeddings for 10 million product descriptions stored in S3. Processing them one-by-one via InvokeModel is too slow and hitting throttling limits. Which Bedrock capability is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Bedrock InvokeModel with increased Lambda concurrency
Bedrock Batch Inference (StartBatchInferenceJob) reading from S3
Bedrock Provisioned Throughput with synchronous invocations
Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoints with auto-scaling

explanation: Bedrock Batch Inference (StartBatchInferenceJob) is purpose-built for large-scale, asynchronous processing of prompts from S3. It optimises cost and throughput by batching requests without per-request API overhead — the right choice for millions of records. Increasing Lambda concurrency still hits per-request throttle limits. Provisioned Throughput reduces throttling for steady traffic but doesn't batch requests. SageMaker endpoints require hosting and managing custom containers.
source_topic: Bedrock Batch Inference for millions of records

question_text: An organisation stores its internal documentation in Confluence and wants to use it as a knowledge source for a Bedrock-powered assistant. They want automatic re-sync when documents are updated in Confluence. What is the SIMPLEST approach?

options.text: Export Confluence pages to S3 manually each week and trigger a Glue ETL job
Use a Bedrock Knowledge Base managed connector for Confluence with scheduled ingestion jobs
Build a custom Lambda scraper that polls the Confluence API and writes to OpenSearch
Use AWS AppFlow to sync Confluence to DynamoDB, then write a custom RAG layer

explanation: Bedrock Knowledge Bases provide managed connectors for SaaS sources including Confluence, SharePoint, and S3. The connector handles authentication, data extraction, chunking, embedding, and indexing — with configurable ingestion schedules for automatic re-sync. Manual exports are error-prone and not automatic. A custom Lambda scraper requires significant build and maintenance effort. AppFlow → DynamoDB → custom RAG adds unnecessary complexity.
source_topic: Bedrock KB managed connector for Confluence

topic: SageMaker Data Wrangler for FM prep
question_text: A data scientist wants to visually profile, detect anomalies, and create data quality reports for a dataset before using it for fine-tuning a foundation model. Which AWS tool provides a UI-driven interface for this workflow?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon QuickSight
AWS Config

explanation: SageMaker Data Wrangler provides a visual, UI-driven interface for data profiling, anomaly detection, and quality reporting — purpose-built for ML/AI dataset preparation. Glue Data Quality uses rule-based checks in an ETL pipeline (code/config-driven). QuickSight is a BI dashboard tool, not a data preparation service. AWS Config monitors resource compliance, not dataset quality.
source_topic: SageMaker Data Wrangler visual data prep
